messages.author: 964993c75887caa8
messages.subject: Covariance matrix with ordered variables
parts:
Dear all,

I want to include the covariance matrix in an article so that readers
can replicate my analysis.

Nevertheless, almost all the variables in the data set are
dichotomous, including the endogenous ones, so in my analysis I've
used the specification ordered= .

I understand that the covariance matrix cannot be used to replicate an
analysis with categorical endogenous variables, but that the complete
data set should be provided. Is that correct?

Many thanks,

Ángel

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Covariance matrix with ordered variables
parts:
Hi Angel,
If all the variables are ordinal, you can condense the raw data into a n-way contingency table.  As easier representation of this to work with might be to aggregate the data to the pattern of values across the variables, with an extra column for the count of cases with that pattern.  If you do that, it is not difficult to write a script or function to dis-aggregate the data.  All the user has to do is write each row as many times as indicated by the count column.

If you have some continuous variables mixed in (too many values to tabulate) then raw data is probably your best option.  If you want to archive it for others to use, the journal might support electronic supplements or it could go in an institutional archive with a link published in the article.  Otherwise, you could simply make it available upon request.  Either way, you need to think about de-indentifying the data to protect participants.  That may require removing some of the demographics.  (If there is no interest in the association between demographics and other variables, I have also seen it suggested that you can randomize the order of the demographics separately from the rest of the data, so that descriptive statistics on the demographics are valid but values cannot be matched to the variables in the study.)  The choices depend on how sensitive the data is.

Keith

Keith A. Markus

http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Covariance matrix with ordered variables
parts: If all the variables are ordinal, you can condense the raw data into a n-way contingency table.  As easier representation of this to work with might be to aggregate the data to the pattern of values across the variables, with an extra column for the count of cases with that pattern.

FYI, you can do this with the lavTables() function.  See the first help-page example:

HS9 <- HolzingerSwineford1939[,c("x1","x2","x3","x4","x5",
                                 "x6","x7","x8","x9")]
HSbinary <- as.data.frame( lapply(HS9, cut, 2, labels=FALSE) )

# counts & proportions for each response pattern
lavTables(HSbinary, dim = 0L, categorical = names(HSbinary))

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Covariance matrix with ordered variables
parts: I understand that the covariance matrix cannot be used to replicate an analysis with categorical endogenous variables

It can in lavaan!   But you need more information than just the polychoric(+polyserial?) correlations.  You also need the thresholds (and means of continuous variables), as well as their sampling variances to use for the weights in DWLS estimation.  A robust estimate of their sampling covariances is also required, to correct the SEs and test statistic.  

This earlier post shows how to extract all the information from a lavaan object, then refit the model to the summary stats:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/aLZJ1Fahrnk/m/uzvI8WrKAQAJ

Since that is certainly too much to simply print in an appendix, I would recommend to save() the R objects in a workspace or each object separately using saveRDS(), then upload them to an OSF project with any other online supplemental materials for your paper.

Of course, you can just provide the table of response patterns, as Keith suggested, which makes this all unnecessary.  Missing data, however, might complicate the situation if you used pairwise deletion.  In  that case,  you should assign NA to a separate category (e.g., -9) so that it is also included in the response patterns.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
